teach.walk2Body: We already know the answer for each {kind, select, grain {seed} cell {cell} blip {reading} other {berry}} here. Put some into the baskets. That is all 'teaching' means.
teach.walk3Title: Then it meets new {kind, select, grain {seeds} cell {cells} blip {readings} other {berries}}
teach.walk3Body: The ? ones are new to it. To guess, it finds the example YOU taught it that looks most like the new one, and copies that answer.
teach.walk4Body: If you only ever show it one kind — only small ones, only light ones — a different-looking one will fool it, and it will be confidently wrong. Pick examples that cover every kind.

help.title: Ask Robo Bunny
help.explainBlockNone: Tap a block in your program first, then I'll explain it.
help.whyFailedNone: Nothing has failed yet — press Run and I'll watch what happens.
help.similarNone: I don't have a smaller example for this one yet — try the hint instead.
help.similarIntro: Here's a smaller puzzle that uses the same idea. Watch it run, then try yours again.
help.failStep: The run stopped at step {step}, while block {number} (“{block}”) was running.
help.failNoStep: The program ran all the way to the end, but the goal wasn't reached.

why.bumped: Robo Bunny hopped into a rock (or off the map). Just before that step it was facing the wrong way — a turn is missing, or points the wrong way.
why.splashed: Robo Bunny hopped into water. The path needed a turn before that tile, or one hop fewer.
why.notOnGoal: Every block ran, but Robo Bunny stopped somewhere else. Count the tiles to the goal and compare with your hops.
why.carrotsLeft: Robo Bunny reached the end but missed something on the way. Which tile did it skip?
why.budget: The program never stopped — a loop kept going with no way to end. Does it need a count, or a goal to stop at?
why.tooManyBlocks: It worked, but with more blocks than the three-star limit. Look for a stretch that repeats — a Repeat block can say it once.
why.missingBlock: This level is about a particular block, and the program didn't use it.
why.forbiddenBlock: The program used a block this level asks you to do without.
why.generic: The run didn't reach the goal. Watch it again and find the first step where Robo Bunny goes somewhere you didn't expect.
why.wrongVariable: Each counter block changes the number by a fixed amount, in order. Write the number after each block and see where it drifts from the target.
why.mazeInvalid: The program never ran, because the maze itself broke a rule on the checklist. Tap “Change my maze”, fix the line without a tick, and build again.
why.genericAnswer: Not quite yet. Read the question again slowly, and check each part of your answer one at a time.
why.wrongOutput: Robo Bunny said something different from what was needed. Check the words in each say block, and whether they happen in the right order.
why.wrongOption: The program does something a little different from the answer you picked. Pretend you are the computer: follow it one line at a time, and keep track of where things are after each line.
why.wrongOrder: Computers do steps in exactly the order they are written. Find the first step that couldn't happen yet, and ask what has to come before it.
why.teachBothBuckets: The bunny learns only from examples. With too few in one basket, it has nothing to compare with, so it can't learn that kind yet.
why.modelGuessedWrong: The bunny copies the answer of the example that looks most like the new one. It guessed wrong because nothing you taught it looks like the ones it missed. Teach it one that does.
why.classifierErrors: Your line decides which side each point belongs to. Some points ended up on the wrong side. Move or turn the line a little and watch which points change sides.
why.trendMissTooHigh: The miss score adds up how far each point is from your line. A line that runs through the middle of the points, not above or below them, misses less.
why.mysteryRoundsWrong: A computer only sees a picture as tiny squares of colour. Look at the pattern of squares, not at what you think the picture shows.
why.pilesNotTight: Things in the same group should be close together. If a group is spread out, it is probably really two groups, or its centre is in the wrong place.
why.tooManyExamples: This level is about teaching well with only a few examples. Choose the ones that cover every kind, and leave the rest out.
why.emptyTrick: A trick is a set of steps with a name. Calling an empty trick does nothing, so fill “my trick” with the steps you want to repeat.
why.didNotRunEnough: A counter only counts when its “add” block runs. If “add” runs once, the counter changes once, even if Robo Bunny hops many times. Put “add” where it runs once for each thing you count.

blocks.bb_whenStart: The start. Everything snapped under this block runs when you press Run — from the top, one block at a time.
blocks.bb_moveForward: One hop in the direction Robo Bunny is facing. It never turns by itself — if there's a rock ahead, it bumps.
blocks.bb_turnLeft: Turns Robo Bunny a quarter turn to its left, on the spot. It doesn't move to a new tile.
blocks.bb_turnRight: Turns Robo Bunny a quarter turn to its right, on the spot. It doesn't move to a new tile.
blocks.bb_collect: Picks up whatever is on the tile Robo Bunny is standing on. It only works while standing ON the item.
blocks.bb_say: Robo Bunny says the words you typed. Useful for messages — it doesn't move anything.
blocks.bb_repeat: Runs everything inside its mouth that many times, in order, before moving on to the block below.
blocks.bb_repeatUntilGoal: Keeps running what's inside until Robo Bunny is standing on the goal — no counting needed. Make sure it can actually get there!
blocks.bb_if: Asks a question first. If the answer is yes, the blocks inside run; if no, they're skipped and the program carries on below.
blocks.bb_ifElse: Asks a question, then does ONE of two things: the first mouth if yes, the second mouth if no. Exactly one of them always runs.
blocks.bb_pathAhead: A sensor question: is the tile in front of Robo Bunny blocked? It answers yes or no — it doesn't move or turn.
blocks.bb_setCounter: Puts a number into the counter — Robo Bunny's one pocket for remembering a number. Setting it replaces whatever was there.
blocks.bb_changeCounter: Adds to the number already in the counter (a minus number takes away). The counter remembers the new total.
blocks.bb_sayCounter: Robo Bunny says the number that is in the counter right now.
blocks.bb_defineTrick: Teaches Robo Bunny a trick: the blocks inside get a name, but they don't run yet. Use “do my trick” to run them — as many times as you like.
blocks.bb_doTrick: Runs the trick you taught, once, right here. Teach it once, use it anywhere.

help.whyWrongNone: Nothing has gone wrong yet. Give it a try, and if it doesn't work I'll explain why.

concept.generic: Every level practises one idea. Read the mission again. It tells you what to aim for, and the hint ladder helps one step at a time.
concept.sequencing: Sequencing means putting steps in the right order. A computer does exactly what it is told, one step after another, and never skips ahead.
concept.loops: A loop repeats the steps inside it. When you see the same steps again and again, a loop says it once and repeats it for you.
concept.conditionals: An if block makes a choice: if something is true, do this, otherwise do that. It lets one program cope with different situations.
concept.logic: Logic is thinking step by step about what must be true. Work out what you know for sure first, then what follows from it.
concept.variables: A variable is a box with a name that remembers a number. You can put a number in, add to it, and read it back later.
concept.functions: A function, or trick, is a set of steps you name once and use many times. Teach the trick once, then call it wherever you need it.
concept.debugging: Debugging means finding and fixing a mistake in a program. Run it, find the first place it does something unexpected, and fix just that.
concept.reading-code: Reading code means working out what a program does before it runs. Follow it line by line, like the computer would.
concept.algorithms: An algorithm is a clear list of steps that always solves a problem. Some algorithms are shorter or faster than others.
concept.classification: Classification means sorting things into groups. An AI learns to sort by looking at examples that people have already sorted.
concept.clustering: Clustering finds groups without being told the answers. Things that are close together probably belong together.
concept.features: Features are the clues a computer uses to decide, like size or colour. Good clues make good decisions.
concept.prediction: A prediction is a careful guess about something new, based on patterns in what we have already seen.
concept.regression: A trend line shows the general direction of the data. It won't touch every point, but it should stay close to most of them.
concept.boundary: A boundary is the line where a decision changes. Points on one side get one answer, and points on the other side get the other.
concept.outliers: An outlier is a data point that doesn't fit with the rest, often a mistake in measuring. It can pull a whole answer off course.
concept.pixels: A picture on a screen is made of tiny squares called pixels. Computers find patterns in those squares.
concept.computer-vision: Computer vision is how computers 'see'. They don't understand a picture like we do. They compare patterns of pixels.
concept.ethics: Ethics means asking what is fair and kind, and who could be helped or hurt when a computer makes a decision.
concept.bias: Bias happens when an AI learns from examples that leave some people or things out. Then it works less well for them.
concept.privacy: Privacy means keeping your personal information, like your address or passwords, safe and shared only with people you trust.
concept.cyber-safety: Staying safe online means stopping to think before you click, share or reply, and telling a trusted adult when something feels wrong.
concept.misinformation: Not everything online is true, and some of it is made by AI. Check who made it, and whether other trusted places say the same.
concept.data: Data is information we collect, like measurements or answers. Good data is careful and complete. Messy data gives messy answers.
concept.sensors: A sensor lets a robot notice the world, like whether the path ahead is blocked. The program decides what to do with what it senses.
concept.robot: A robot follows its program exactly. It can't guess what you meant, so every step has to be there.
concept.creative: This is your own creation. There is more than one good answer. Plan it, try it, and improve it.
concept.evaluation: Testing an AI means checking it on examples it has never seen. That is the only fair way to know how well it learned.

misconceptions.heading: Common mistakes to reteach
misconceptions.caveat: The ideas behind this class's failed runs in the last 30 days, with a suggestion for the board. Aggregates only — no child is named.
misconceptions.meta: {attempts, plural, one {# run} other {# runs}} · {students, plural, one {# child} other {# children}}

turnDirection.label: Left and right from the bunny's view
turnDirection.reteach: Runs ended in a bump right after a turn. Have children stand and turn their own bodies the way Robo Bunny faces, then say the turn before placing the block.

hazardAhead.label: Not checking the tile ahead
hazardAhead.reteach: Robo Bunny hopped into water. Trace the route on the map with a finger before building, one tile per hop.

countingHops.label: Counting the tiles
countingHops.reteach: Every block ran and the bunny stopped short or went past. Count squares aloud, not including the one it stands on, and match the count to blocks.

missedStop.label: Routes that skip an item
missedStop.reteach: The burrow was reached but something was left behind. Plan the route as legs — first stop, second stop, then the burrow — before the first block.

loopNeverEnds.label: Loops with no way to end
loopNeverEnds.reteach: 'Repeat until I reach the goal' kept going because the goal was never reachable from that program. Ask: what has to be true for the loop to stop?

repeatNotUsed.label: Repetition written out by hand
repeatNotUsed.reteach: Passes over the block budget: the same blocks in a row instead of a Repeat. Circle the repeating stretch on a printed program and rewrite it as one loop.

sayPlacement.label: Where a block sits in a loop
sayPlacement.reteach: The bunny said the wrong words — usually a 'say' inside the loop instead of after it. Act it out: inside the loop means every time round.

counterTrace.label: Following the counter
counterTrace.reteach: The counter ended on the wrong number. Trace on paper: write its value after every block, starting from what it was set to.

requiredBlock.label: The block the level asked for
requiredBlock.reteach: Solved another way, without the block being practised. Show both solutions side by side and ask which one still works if the map gets longer.

readingCode.label: Reading a program before it runs
readingCode.reteach: Wrong predictions in Code City. Read a short program aloud as a class, one line at a time, and move a bunny on a paper grid.

sequencing.label: Putting steps in order
sequencing.reteach: Steps were placed out of order. Try an unplugged version: sequence a snack recipe on cards, then check what breaks when two swap.

mazeDesign.label: Designing a maze that can be solved
mazeDesign.reteach: Maze designs broke a checklist rule. Have pairs swap paper mazes and test each other's before building on screen.

learnGap.label: The Learn-step gap
learnGap.reteach: The wrong block was tried in a lesson's gap. Replay the worked example on the projector and ask what the missing block changes.

classifierExamples.label: Choosing teaching examples
classifierExamples.reteach: The taught machine misread the held-out berries. Discuss which examples were missing — the rare ones decide.

trendFit.label: Fitting a line to points
trendFit.reteach: Trend lines missed the least-squares fit by too much. Ask where the line should sit so as many points are above as below.

groupingFlags.label: Placing group flags
groupingFlags.reteach: Flags landed between crowds. Look at the board before placing: how many crowds, and where is the middle of each?

reflections.heading: How the class felt
reflections.caveat: From the one-tap question after each level: the levels this class most often called tricky, once at least 5 children have answered. Shown as a rough share and updated once a day, so no child's answer can be worked out.

interventions.heading: Suggested next steps
interventions.caveat: Worked out from this student's attempts, hints and activity. You know them; this only knows their work.

REVIEW_CONCEPT.title: Review the idea behind this level together
REVIEW_CONCEPT.evidence: {attempts, plural, one {# attempt} other {# attempts}} on {level}, and the last three all failed.
REVIEW_CONCEPT.suggestion: Repeated failure on one level usually means the idea has not landed yet, not that they are not trying. A few minutes on the concept is likely to unblock the rest of the world.

HINT_RELIANCE.title: Check they can work without the last hint
HINT_RELIANCE.evidence: Needed the final hint tier on {levels, plural, one {# level} other {# levels}}.
HINT_RELIANCE.suggestion: Reaching the deepest hint on several levels can mean a gap earlier in the sequence. Try watching them start one level unaided to see where they stall.

PACING.title: They are getting there, slowly
PACING.evidence: About {minutes} minutes on {level}, which is planned for around {estimatedMinutes}.
PACING.suggestion: Worth a look at whether the time is thinking, re-reading, or fiddling. Slow and correct is fine; slow and lost is not.

CHECK_IN.title: Check in — they have gone quiet
CHECK_IN.evidence: No activity for {days, plural, =0 {several school days} one {# school day} other {# school days}}, while there is work outstanding.
CHECK_IN.suggestion: A short conversation usually finds the reason faster than more assignments will: a forgotten password and lost confidence look identical from here.

GET_STARTED.title: Help them start
GET_STARTED.suggestion: Sitting with them through the first level tends to be enough. Check they can sign in before assuming they chose not to.

curriculum.cstaNote: Standards codes are our suggested alignment with the CSTA K–12 Computer Science Standards (1B = grades 3–5, 2 = grades 6–8), not an endorsement by CSTA.

csta.1B-AP-08: Compare and refine different algorithms for the same task
csta.1B-AP-09: Use variables to store and change data in a program
csta.1B-AP-10: Build programs with sequences, events, loops and conditionals
csta.1B-AP-11: Break a problem into smaller parts
csta.1B-AP-13: Plan and build a program step by step, improving it as you go
csta.1B-AP-15: Test and debug a program so it works as intended
csta.1B-AP-17: Explain the choices made while building a program
csta.1B-CS-02: Model how hardware and software work together
csta.1B-DA-06: Organise data and show it visually
csta.1B-DA-07: Use data to spot patterns, predict outcomes and explain ideas
csta.1B-IC-20: Seek different perspectives to improve what we build
csta.1B-NI-05: Discuss online safety and how to protect personal information
csta.2-AP-11: Create clearly named variables and operate on their values
csta.2-AP-12: Combine control structures, including nested loops and conditionals
csta.2-AP-13: Decompose problems into parts to design programs
csta.2-AP-17: Test and refine programs systematically with different cases
csta.2-CS-02: Combine hardware and software to collect and exchange data
csta.2-DA-07: Represent data in more than one way
csta.2-DA-08: Collect and clean data to make it more useful and reliable
csta.2-DA-09: Refine a model using the data it produces
csta.2-IC-20: Weigh how technology affects people's everyday lives
csta.2-IC-21: Discuss bias and accessibility in technology design
csta.2-IC-23: Weigh keeping information public versus private and secure
